The SIR model of [Tutorial 1](t1_intro.qmd) and [Tutorial 2](t2_model.qmd) is over within weeks, far faster than real measles. [Tutorial 2](t2_model.qmd) found that R0 and prior immunity decide how *many* people are infected. This tutorial asks: **what decides how *fast* an outbreak spreads?** It adds, one at a time, structure that most disease models need, comparing the epidemic with and without each:

- a latent period, in which people are infected but not yet infectious;
- the distribution of the time people spend in a state, not just its average;
- immunity that wanes;
- a branch, where people in one state go one of two ways (here, a small share die).

It then names the parameters, checks the finished disease, and runs it as agents, where chance and differences between people matter. By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

- turn an SIR model into an SEIR model, and say why it changes the course of the epidemic but not R0;
- choose the distribution of a duration;
- add waning immunity and deaths;
- name parameters, with a description and a range of plausible values;
- check a disease from its description, equations, and diagram;
- run a disease as agents, and see how chance and differences between people (superspreading) decide whether one case starts an outbreak.

## A latent period

People infected with measles become infectious about 10 days later. In an SEIR model, people in this latent period are in their own compartment, E (exposed): infected, but not yet infectious. Infection moves people from S to E, and progression from E to I.

Here are the SIR and SEIR models, run for 150 days. Both diseases are named `measles`, so their results can be plotted together:

```{python}
import starsim as ss

# The SIR model of Tutorials 1 and 2
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
sir = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')

# The SEIR model: infection leads to E, not I
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I        # Infected by contact with infectious people, I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Infectious after a latent period of 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Recovered after 8 days on average
seir = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')

sir_sim  = ss.Sim(sir,  total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
seir_sim = ss.Sim(seir, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
msim = ss.parallel({'SIR': sir_sim, 'SEIR': seir_sim})
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

Only `I` is infectious, since only it appears in the rate of infection. Both outbreaks start with 0.1% infectious (`init=dict(I=0.001)`; `init_prev=0.001` would put them in `E`, [Tutorial 2](t2_model.qmd)).

R0 is the same in both, 15.2: it depends on how many people each infectious person infects (β = 1.9 a day, for 8 days), not on how soon they become infectious. But with a latent period, the time from one infection to the next (the generation time) is about 18 days instead of 8, so the epidemic peaks on day 28 rather than day 6, and lower (29,000 infectious at once rather than 74,000). Almost everyone is still infected, since that depends on R0. So the first answer is the generation time: for the same R0, a longer one means a slower, flatter epidemic.

## How long people stay in a state

A duration such as `ss.days(10)` is an average; by default, the time in the state is exponentially distributed, as in the standard ODE. That describes most latent periods poorly: with a mean of 10 days, 10% of people become infectious within a day, and 12% are still not infectious after three weeks. The latent period of measles varies much less.

A duration can be any distribution. An Erlang distribution (a gamma with a whole-number shape, `k`) is the usual choice in compartmental models. With `k=10`, the latent period still averages 10 days, with a standard deviation of about 3. Here it is, against the exponential latent period:

```{python}
progression = E >> I @ ss.erlang(k=10, mean=ss.days(10))  # 10 days on average; 95% between 5 and 17
seir_erlang = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')

erlang_sim = ss.Sim(seir_erlang, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
msim = ss.parallel({'Exponential latent period': seir_sim, 'Erlang latent period': erlang_sim})
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

R0 is the same, but the epidemic peaks two weeks later, on day 44, and higher (35,000 infectious rather than 29,000). With an exponential latent period, the few who become infectious within a day or two start chains of infection early, speeding up the epidemic; with an Erlang one, almost nobody does. So the distribution of a duration, not just its average, sets how fast an epidemic grows: worth knowing when fitting a model to early growth.

As an ODE, Starsim runs an Erlang distribution as `k` exponential stages in a row, each 1/`k` of the mean. The stages are not separate conditions of the disease, only a way to narrow the time in `E`. Written out, the Erlang latent period is a transition with 10 stages:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
progression = E >> I @ ss.erlang(k=10, mean=ss.days(10))
```

## R

```r
progression <- Transition(E, I, dur = ss$erlang(k = 10, mean = days(10)))
```

## Explicit

```{python}
progression = ss.Transition(source=E, dest=I, dur=ss.days(10), stages=10) # 10 exponential stages of 1 day each, on average
```
:::

`equations()` shows the stages, as `E_1` to `E_10`:

```{python}
seir_erlang.equations()
```

As agents, each person draws their own time from the distribution instead. Other distributions, such as `ss.lognormal(mean=ss.days(10), std=ss.days(2))`, are covered in [Distributions](../user_guide/mechanics_distributions.qmd). The rest of the tutorials keep to exponential durations.

## Waning immunity

So far, people who recover are immune for life, as after measles. For many infections, such as pertussis, RSV, or cholera, immunity wanes, a transition from `R` back to `S`: an SEIRS model. Suppose (unlike real measles) that immunity lasted 2 years on average, and run both models for 5 years:

```{python}
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Back to an exponential latent period
waning      = R >> S @ ss.years(2)  # Susceptible again after 2 years on average
seirs = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, waning, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')

lifelong = ss.Sim(seir,  total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.years(5), unit='day')
waning_sim = ss.Sim(seirs, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.years(5), unit='day')
msim = ss.parallel({'Lifelong immunity': lifelong, 'Immunity lasting 2 years': waning_sim})
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

With durations in days and years, `unit='day'` says which unit the bare β = 1.9 is in ([Tutorial 2](t2_model.qmd)). The first outbreak is the same in both. With lifelong immunity, it is the only one, and the disease dies out. With waning immunity, smaller waves follow, settling to about 1,000 people infectious at any time: the disease becomes endemic. A supply of new susceptible people, from waning immunity or births ([Tutorial 6](t6_data.qmd#births-and-deaths)), is what lets an infection persist rather than burn out.

## Deaths: a branch

A small share of people with measles die, from complications such as pneumonia: from 1 in 1,000 cases or fewer in high-income countries to several in 100 in some low-income settings. Suppose it is 2 in 1,000. People leaving `I` then branch: 99.8% recover and 0.2% die. A branch is a transition with `p=`, the share that take it:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(8), p=0.998)        # 99.8% recover...
death       = ss.Transition(I, ss.dead, dur=ss.days(8), p=0.002)  # ...and 0.2% die
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, death, init=dict(I=0.001))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
sim.run()
print('Deaths:', round(sim.results.measles.death.sum()))
```

## R

```r
library(starsim)

states("S E I R")
measles <- Disease(
  infection   = Transition(S, E, rate = 1.9 * I),
  progression = Transition(E, I, dur = days(10)),
  recovery    = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8), p = 0.998),       # 99.8% recover...
  death       = Transition(I, ss$dead, dur = days(8), p = 0.002), # ...and 0.2% die
  init = list(I = 0.001)
)

sim <- Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, stop = days(150))
sim$run()
cat("Deaths:", round(sum(sim$results$measles$death$values)), "\n")
```

## Explicit

```{python}
S, E, I, R = ss.State(name='S'), ss.State(name='E'), ss.State(name='I'), ss.State(name='R')
measles_explicit = ss.Disease(
    transitions = [
        ss.Transition(source=S, dest=E, rate=ss.perday(1.9)*I, name='infection'),
        ss.Transition(source=E, dest=I, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(10)), name='progression'),
        ss.Transition(source=I, dest=R, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(8)), p=0.998, name='recovery'),    # 99.8% recover...
        ss.Transition(source=I, dest=ss.dead, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(8)), p=0.002, name='death'), # ...and 0.2% die
    ],
    init = dict(S=0.999, I=0.001), # The share of people in each state at the start
    name = 'measles',
)

sim_explicit = ss.Sim(diseases=measles_explicit, networks=ss.contacts(1), total_pop=100_000, start=ss.days(0), stop=ss.days(150), dt=ss.days(1), unit='day', solver='ode')
sim_explicit.run()
print('Deaths:', round(sim_explicit.results.measles.death.sum()))
```
:::

`ss.dead` is outside the model: people who die leave the population. Each branch has its own result (`recovery` and `death`), and could have its own duration. Almost everyone is infected, so about 0.2% of 100,000 people die, too few to change the epidemic. In the equations, who goes which way is decided on entering `I`, so `I` is in two parts, `I_1` (who will recover) and `I_2` (who will die):

```{python}
measles.equations()
```

Two transitions out of a state with rates (or durations) and no `p=` are instead competing risks: whichever happens first moves each person, so the rates set the shares. A branch gives the share directly, which is how the case fatality ratio is usually known. Use whichever matches what you know.

The next tutorials leave deaths out, since they change little else here.

## Naming the parameters

Starsim names parameters itself (`beta`, `dur_E`, ...), as [Tutorial 2](t2_model.qmd) showed. To name them yourself, use `ss.par()`. Each takes its name from its variable, and can have a description (`doc=`), a source (`source=`), and bounds, the range of plausible values:

```{python}
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta           = ss.par(1.9, bounds=[1, 3], doc='Transmission rate per day')
dur_latent     = ss.par(ss.days(10), bounds=[ss.days(7), ss.days(14)], doc='Average latent period', source='Assumed for this tutorial')
dur_infectious = ss.par(ss.days(8), doc='Average infectious period')

infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
progression = E >> I @ dur_latent
recovery    = ss.Transition(I, R, dur=dur_infectious, p=0.998)
death       = ss.Transition(I, ss.dead, dur=dur_infectious, p=0.002)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, death, init=dict(I=0.001))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
```

One parameter can be used in several places, as `dur_infectious` is, and changing it changes it everywhere: `ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(dur_latent=ss.days(12)), ...)` runs with a 12-day latent period. [Calibration](t6_data.qmd#fitting-and-checking-the-fit) uses the bounds: `sim.fit()` searches for the values of every bounded parameter that best match data. See [Parameters](../user_guide/building_parameters.qmd) for more, including priors.

## Checking the disease

With four states and four transitions, check that the disease is what you meant before using it. `describe()` lists every state, transition, and parameter as built: which states are infectious, the distribution of each duration, each parameter with its value, bounds, description, and source, and every value Starsim chose itself, marked as guessed:

```{python}
sim.describe()
```

`equations()` gives the ODEs, the quickest way to check that every flow leaves one state and enters another, and that the force of infection is what you meant:

```{python}
measles.equations()
```

`diagram()` draws a flowchart, with the transmission dashed, an empty circle for `ss.dead`, and each arrow labeled with its value and, for a branch, its share:

```{python}
measles.diagram()
```

`measles.diagram('text')` gives it as a Mermaid flowchart instead, which JupyterLab, Quarto, GitHub, and many other tools draw.

A disease can also be written as a class, with its states, parameters, and transitions in the class body: worth doing for a disease used in several models or shared, since it can then be made with other parameter values, like the diseases in Starsim's library (e.g. `Measles(beta=1.5)`). [Diseases](../user_guide/building_diseases.qmd) in the user guide shows how, with other kinds of transition, such as those triggered by an event.

## As agents

Everything above also runs as agents (with `n_agents=`, as in [Tutorial 1](t1_intro.qmd)). Each person then has their own state, their own times of moving between states, and, if you want, their own infectiousness and susceptibility. This shows what a compartmental model can't: each person's durations, chance when cases are few, and differences between people.

### Each person's latent period

Above, an Erlang latent period changed the epidemic, compared with an exponential one of the same mean. As agents, you can see why, since each person draws their own:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection = S >> E @ 1.9*I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
latent_periods = {'Exponential': ss.days(10), 'Erlang (k = 10)': ss.erlang(k=10, mean=ss.days(10))}
agent_sims = {}
for label, latent in latent_periods.items():
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, E >> I @ latent, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001), name='measles')
    agent_sims[label] = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(150), verbose=0)
ss.parallel(agent_sims)

plt.figure()
for label, s in agent_sims.items():
    latent = s.diseases.measles.E.stays # How long each person who has been through E stayed there: their latent period, in days
    print(f'{label}: mean latent period {np.mean(latent):.1f} days')
    plt.hist(latent, bins=np.arange(0, 40), alpha=0.5, label=label)
plt.xlabel('Latent period (days)')
plt.ylabel('Number of people')
plt.legend();
```

With an exponential latent period, short ones are the most common, and many take three weeks or more; with an Erlang distribution, most people become infectious 6 to 17 days after infection. Both average about 10 days, in whole days since agents move in whole steps. `E.stays` covers everyone who has entered and left E. (Subtracting `m.ti_I - m.ti_E` would give a day more, since an infection happens at the end of its step and becoming infectious at the start of one.)

### Chance, and the first case

In a compartmental model, an infection with R above 1 always takes off. In reality, the first cases may recover before infecting anyone, and the outbreak dies out by chance. Agents capture this.

Suppose 90% of the town is immune, as in the towns of later tutorials, and one infectious person arrives. Each case then infects about 1.9 × 8 × 0.1 ≈ 1.5 others. Here are 20 runs as agents, each with its own random seed and line (`lines=True`), and the ODE for comparison:

```{python}
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=1)) # 90% immune, and 1 case

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(365), verbose=0)
msim = ss.parallel(ss.Sim(measles, **pars), n_runs=20)
msim.plot('measles.I', lines=True)

ode = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=5000, stop=ss.days(365), solver='ode', verbose=0)
ode.run()
ode.plot('measles.I')
```

The ODE always gives the same outbreak. As agents, some runs give one about as large, and the rest die out after a handful of cases. Counting runs with fewer than 20 infections:

```{python}
total = msim.results.measles.infection.values.sum(axis=1) # Total infections in each run
print('Share of introductions that die out:', np.mean(total < 20))
```

Theory says one case dies out with a chance of 1/R (for an exponential infectious period), here about 2 in 3, close to the runs. This matters for questions about introductions: how likely an imported case is to start an outbreak, or how long a place stays free of a disease.

### People who differ: superspreading

For many diseases, most cases infect few others or none, and a few infect many (superspreading). This is usually described by giving each person an infectiousness drawn from a gamma distribution with mean 1 and shape (dispersion) k: the smaller k, the more transmission is concentrated (SARS in 2003 had k near 0.16).

A value that each person has is an attribute, `ss.attr()`: here, drawn once for each person when they are made (a trait). `ss.modify()` then multiplies each person's infectiousness (`rel_trans`) by it:

```{python}
def make_sim(k=None):
    """ The measles model, with the infectiousness of each person drawn from a gamma distribution with shape k """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    if k is None: # Everyone equally infectious
        measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=1))
        return ss.Sim(measles, **pars)
    infectiousness = ss.attr(ss.gamma(shape=k, scale=1/k)) # A mean of 1, and a shape (dispersion) of k
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, infectiousness=infectiousness, init=dict(R=0.9), init_n=dict(I=1))
    superspreading = ss.modify(measles.rel_trans, multiply=infectiousness)
    return ss.Sim(measles, connectors=superspreading, **pars)

for label, k in {'Everyone equally infectious': None, 'k = 1': 1, 'k = 0.2': 0.2}.items():
    msim = ss.parallel(make_sim(k), n_runs=40)
    total = msim.results.measles.infection.values.sum(axis=1)
    print(label, '- share that die out:', np.mean(total < 20), '- median size of the outbreaks that take off:', np.median(total[total >= 20]))
```

Each case infects about 1.5 others on average in all three, but the more concentrated transmission is, the more often an introduction dies out: with k = 0.2, about 4 in 5 do, since the first case is most likely one who infects nobody. The outbreaks that take off are of similar size, but can start explosively, from a single event. A compartmental model can't show this, having no individuals to differ.

`ss.attr()` can also draw a value when something happens to a person (e.g. a severity at infection, with `when=infection`), or record one; see [Diseases](../user_guide/building_diseases.qmd). Susceptibility can differ in the same way, with `ss.modify(measles.rel_sus, ...)`.

### Counting each person's infections

With waning immunity, people can be infected again and again. Here is an SIRS model of a generic respiratory infection (R0 = 0.4 × 7 = 2.8) with immunity lasting 6 months on average, over three years. The attribute `infections` counts each person's infections (`combine='sum'` adds 1 at each): a history, which only agents have:

```{python}
def make_cold():
    """ A respiratory infection whose immunity wanes, counting each person's infections """
    S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ 0.4*I        # β = 0.4 per day
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(7)   # Infectious for 7 days on average
    waning    = R >> S @ ss.days(180) # Immune for 6 months on average
    infections = ss.attr(1, when=infection, combine='sum', init=0) # The number of times each person has been infected
    return ss.Disease(infection, recovery, waning, infections=infections, init_prev=0.01, name='cold')

pars_cold = dict(n_agents=5000, stop=ss.days(3*365), verbose=0)
sirs = ss.Sim(make_cold(), **pars_cold)
sirs.run()
sirs.plot('cold.I')
```

As with waning immunity above, the infection returns in waves that settle at an endemic level. An analyzer that adds 1 for each person infected in each step (`cold.infection.uids`) gives exactly the same counts as the attribute. After three years:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
counts = sirs.people.cold.infections.values
plt.figure()
plt.hist(counts, bins=np.arange(counts.max() + 2) - 0.5)
plt.xlabel('Number of infections in 3 years')
plt.ylabel('Number of people');
```

## Explicit

```{python}
class CountInfections(ss.Analyzer):
    """ The number of times each person has been infected, counted by hand """
    def init_post(self):
        super().init_post()
        self.counts = np.zeros(len(self.sim.people), dtype=int)
        self.counts[self.sim.diseases.cold.I.uids] = 1 # The people infectious at the start
    def step(self):
        self.counts[self.sim.diseases.cold.infection.uids] += 1 # The people infected in this step

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
cold = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.4*I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(7), waning=R >> S @ ss.days(180), init_prev=0.01) # No attribute
counted = ss.Sim(cold, analyzers=CountInfections(), **pars_cold)
counted.run()

counts = counted.analyzers.countinfections.counts
plt.figure()
plt.hist(counts, bins=np.arange(counts.max() + 2) - 0.5)
plt.xlabel('Number of infections in 3 years')
plt.ylabel('Number of people');
```
:::

Everyone is infected at least once, most people 3 to 5 times, varying by chance. A model can use a person's history: e.g. `ss.modify(cold.rel_sus, multiply=0.5, who=cold.infection.n_times >= 2)` would halve the susceptibility of people infected at least twice.

Every disease here is declared, as states and transitions. A disease can also be written as Python code, a class whose methods say what happens to each agent at each step, as in Starsim 3: [T8 – Custom modules](t8_modules.qmd#a-disease-written-as-code) shows how. [Tutorial 4](t4_mixing.qmd) splits the town of the SEIR model (without deaths) into age groups.

## Exercises

1. Measles has a latent period of 10 to 12 days. Using the model with named parameters, run it with a latent period of 12 days, using `pars=`. Does R0 change? How do the timing and height of the peak change?
2. Give the infectious period an Erlang distribution too, with `k=4`. Using `R0()` and a plot of `I`, check whether R0 or the course of the epidemic changes.
3. About 1 in 10 people with measles in this town are admitted to hospital, after 4 days of being infectious on average, and stay for 7 days. Add a state for people in hospital (assume they don't transmit), and find the largest number of people in hospital at once.
4. Try different durations of immunity in the SIRS model of the respiratory infection (e.g. 1, 6, and 24 months). How do they affect the epidemic curve, and the number of times people are infected?
5. Add a latent period of 2 days to that SIRS model, to make an SEIRS model. Does it change the endemic level?
6. In the town with 90% immune, increase the share susceptible to 20% (`init=dict(R=0.8)`), so that each case infects about 3 others. What share of introductions die out now, with and without superspreading (k = 0.2)?

[Solutions](solutions.qmd#t3-building-a-disease) · Next: [T4 – Mixing](t4_mixing.qmd)

## Further reading

- [Wearing, Rohani & Keeling (2005): Appropriate models for the management of infectious diseases](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.0020174): why exponential latent and infectious periods mislead, and how Erlang stages fix it
- [CDC Pink Book: Measles](https://www.cdc.gov/pinkbook/hcp/table-of-contents/chapter-13-measles.html): the natural history of measles, including its incubation and infectious periods and complications
- [WHO: Measles fact sheet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/measles): deaths from measles, and how they vary between settings
- [Wikipedia: Compartmental models in epidemiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compartmental_models_in_epidemiology): the SEIR and SEIRS models, among others
- [Lloyd-Smith et al. (2005): Superspreading and the effect of individual variation on disease emergence](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04153): the paper that introduced the dispersion k
